\chapter{Which Way Is the Arrow Pointing?}
\label{ch:por-para-contrast}
\hlchaptermodality{161}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose between por and para with one question instead of a list of rules.}

Complete ES-C51-la-flecha: contrast para ti with por ti and state the arrow test.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[por vs para]{Which way is the arrow pointing?}

\label{lesson:ES-C51-la-flecha}



\begin{quote}
One points forward at a target. One points back at a cause. Say which is which before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same sentence, twice}]
The pair that makes the difference visible:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Lo hago \textbf{para} ti.} — I'm doing it \textbf{for} you. \emph{(you receive it)} \emph{Lo hago \textbf{por} ti.} — I'm doing it \textbf{because of} you. \emph{(you are the reason)}
\end{quote}

Two letters apart, and two different sentences about your relationship with somebody. The first is a gift; the second is a motive.

English says \emph{for} in both and lets context carry the rest. Spanish makes you choose, and once you hear the choice you notice English was hiding it.

\textbf{The test:}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Draw an arrow. Does it point at the thing (\emph{para}), or come from it (\emph{por})?}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Es para ti} — arrow \textbf{at} you. You get it.
  \item \emph{Es por ti} — arrow \textbf{from} you. You caused it.
\end{itemize}

That is the whole rung: one arrow, two directions.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The test works because it is not a trick. It is what the two words are made of: \emph{para} contains \textbf{ad} (\textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}), \emph{por} contains \textbf{per} (\textquotedblleft{}through\textquotedblright{}).

You are not memorising which preposition suits which situation. You are reading a direction built into each word before Spanish existed.

That keeps working on uses this book never showed you: meeting \emph{por} in an unfamiliar sentence, ask what it comes \textbf{through} or \textbf{because of}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}Lo hago para ti\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Lo hago por ti\textquotedblright{} — two letters, two relationships
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the arrow arrives before the word does.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Para ti} — who gets it? (\textbf{You do}.) \emph{Por ti} — who caused it? (\textbf{You did}.) And why does the test keep working on sentences this book never showed you? (Because the directions are \textbf{inside the words}.) Next: both in one place.
\end{tcolorbox}
